items.originalTitle: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.author: Adam Wren
items.title: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.summary: Allies of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are launching an independent, grassroots effort urging him to undertake a second presidential campaign ahead of 2028. Team Pete PAC will be led by Jennifer Holdsworth, the former national campaign manager of Buttigieg’s unsuccessful 2017 bid for DNC chair, and Mohsin Syed, his former chief of staff at the Transportation Department. The PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid. “Mohsin and I have traveled the country this year, and everywhere we go, people ask us the same question: how can I help Pete?” Holdsworth said in a statement. Team Pete PAC is independent and has no ties to Buttigieg’s Win the Era PAC, nor is it a presidential committee. Through Win the Era, Buttigieg campaigned with 102 candidates across the map for the midterms, visiting 38 states (19 of them twice). Asked on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday whether he had a timeline to make a decision, Buttigieg said he would be “surprised” if he was the first potential 2028 presidential candidate “to make news” and said he’s “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.” Even as it forms to press Buttigieg to mount a second presidential campaign, Team Pete PAC is urging potential backers to take part in community service — a nod to Buttigeig’s proposed national service program he proposed as a candidate. “I’ve seen up close what Pete can do,” Syed said. “He has a unique ability to bring people together and inspire action.”

items.originalTitle: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.author: Lauren Fedor
items.title: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.summary: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.” “A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.” When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums.. “When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said. “When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.” Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy. “To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.” Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

items.originalTitle: When People Keep What Surgeons Remove
items.author: Angela Haupt
items.title: When People Keep What Surgeons Remove
items.summary: —Photo-Illustration by TIME (Source Images: Olga Pankova—Getty Images, Trygve Finkelsen—Getty Images) Emily likes her uterus much better in a jar than in her body. The 20-year-old, who asked to be identified by her first name to protect her privacy, keeps it in her bedroom, on what she calls her “dead things table,” among animal skulls and other specimens. After years of difficult symptoms, she had a hysterectomy at 19—and made arrangements to bring the organ home. Her mother supplied a sticker that borrows a lyric from a popular Taylor Swift song: “It’s me, hi, I’m the problem, it’s me.” Keeping it is a kind of revenge, Emily explains: “You tortured me, and now you’re chopped up in little bits.” It’s also a bit of inspiration. “There’s a lot of things I know that I can’t control and I cannot fix,” she says. Her uterus, though, “was something I could get fixed.” Other patients have found their own reasons not to part with their body parts. One artist turned his wisdom teeth into calligraphy tools; a man gave a piece of his removed medical tubing to his future wife. Surgeons field requests for everything from breast implants to eyelid skin. Patients have been asking to keep what surgeons remove for decades: Medical literature addressed returning tissue samples as early as 1995 . But research on how often it happens remains limited. A 2019 study found that 22 patients signed specimen-release forms at one Arizona medical center from 2015 to 2017. When researchers interviewed eight of the people, they revealed motivations ranging from curiosity and a desire for a souvenir to honoring cultural beliefs and finding comfort after a loss. The authors described the practice as “poorly tracked and underreported,” and their study did not establish how common it was nationally. Whatever draws patients to these keepsakes, getting one home can require more than asking the surgeon to save it. What makes people want to keep something they need to have removed—and who decides whether they can? Why people keep body parts after surgery Leah Paul had mixed feelings about having her fallopian tubes removed. But she didn’t need to think twice about bringing them home. The 39-year-old Miami-based midwife had spent years living with debilitating Stage 4 endometriosis. She and her surgeon, Dr. Robyn Power, planned an operation to remove endometriosis tissue and her fallopian tubes while trying to preserve her ovaries. Paul wasn’t planning to have more children, but she still needed to talk the decision through with her loved ones. “These fallopian tubes carried the one egg that became my beautiful, incredible 21-year-old daughter,” she says. In her work at Tree of Life Midwifery in Fredericksburg, Va., Paul routinely asks patients whether they want to save their placentas. “You grew that organ, it’s yours,” she says. Keeping a piece of her own body felt right to her. She and her fiancé are artists, and she wanted to turn her tubes into something meaningful. “Dr. Power didn’t even blink,” she says. Paul’s experience with families keeping placentas reflects a practice researchers have documented. In a 2013 survey of perinatal pathologists in the U.S. and Canada, 22 of the 36 respondents said they allowed placentas to be released to families. (These are specialists who examine placentas and other tissues to help understand conditions affecting pregnancy and newborns, like infections or problems with fetal growth.) The most common reason patients requested their placentas was burial. For some families, that practice carries cultural meaning: In Māori tradition in New Zealand , for instance, burying the placenta in a significant place affirms a child’s connection to the land. Power, a gynecologic surgeon with Pelvic Rehabilitation Medicine in South Florida, makes room for these types of conversations when preparing patients for surgery. Some feel little attachment to the tissue being removed. Some want it gone. For others, it’s part of their identity, and letting it go can be difficult even when they want the surgery. “It means something different to everybody,” she says. Only a small percentage of her patients pursue taking specimens home: Power estimates that in the past year, about five expressed interest and completed the necessary paperwork. But she’s noticed more patients asking whether it’s an option in recent years. She suspects greater public awareness of endometriosis and conversations about changing reproductive rights have encouraged patients to ask more questions about their bodily autonomy and reproductive organs. Sometimes, patients want something to show for what they’ve endured, she adds. Power has fielded requests to take home pieces of endometriosis tissue—a physical reminder of the pain that disrupted their lives. “It’s proof,” she says. Even tissue that’s caused misery can be hard to part with. Dr. Elvira Lang, an interventional radiologist and author of Managing Your Medical Experience , recalls a patient who began crying after a procedure to shrink her uterine fibroids. They had caused problems, but they were still part of her body. The experience prompted Lang to start talking with other patients about how they might feel about losing tissue, even when treatment would help them. When Lang had her own hip replaced, she asked to see the removed portion so she could thank it. She didn’t want to bring it home. She wanted a goodbye. “Thank you very much. You did good,” she remembers telling it. “But you know it was time to go.” Sometimes, seeing is enough. In a small British study in 2005 , 33 of the 47 patients who had undergone hysterectomies at Walsall Hospitals NHS Trust in England said they wanted to take a look at their removed uterus, although only 14 visited the laboratory. All 14 who did said the experience helped them understand why they had needed surgery and what happened to the tissue afterward. For comedian Joe Tidd, a piece of medical tubing became an unlikely romantic keepsake. After a serious rugby injury and a subsequent infection, he needed a PICC line to deliver antibiotics, with daily hospital visits to have a pump changed. Hoping to cheer himself up—and perhaps find some stand-up material—he downloaded Tinder and set his search radius to a mile. Maybe he’d meet a nurse. He met his future wife instead. She wasn’t a nurse; she just happened to be passing by the hospital as he was busy swiping. Shortly before their first date, his line came out. After staff stepped away, Tidd says, he retrieved a piece from the trash and saved it. Later, once they’d fallen in love, he gave it to her. “It was a weird thing to do, but she still has it, so I don’t know,” he says. To him, the connection was clear: “My struggles are what led me to her,” he says. “She should have that.” What people do with their medical souvenirs As Anthony Elder prepared to have his wisdom teeth removed at 35, he started considering their potential. There was a family precedent for keeping teeth: His mother had saved his baby teeth in a pill bottle, intending to make a necklace. She never got around to it, he says, but the idea made his own request feel less unusual. Elder, an artist and calligrapher who describes himself as an “oddities appreciator,” asked to keep his teeth at his consultation, then made sure the staff remembered on extraction day. As he came out of anesthesia, he had one pressing question: “Where’s my teeth?” He took them home and figured out how to turn one into a pen. He found writing with something that used to live inside his head uniquely satisfying. “I don’t know how many people have done this,” he says. Tooth keepsakes are familiar territory for Dr. Liel Grinbaum, a pediatric dentist in New York. Some parents save a child’s first lost tooth alongside a lock of hair and a record of their age; others do the same with the last baby tooth, marking the passage out of childhood. He recalls one mother who made tooth earrings, necklaces, and bracelets. His younger patients are often enthusiastic about taking an extracted tooth home, too. Grinbaum helps them write a letter to the tooth fairy and supplies a special box. He also has an incentive ready: “If I had to take it out, the tooth fairy usually pays double.” Adults’ requests extend well beyond the mouth. Dr. Frank Agullo, a plastic surgeon in El Paso, Texas, says patients ask to keep removed breast implants, excised moles, excess eyelid skin, and tissue removed during labiaplasty. Some want to see the specimen or a photograph, and that’s enough, while others are already clearing space on their shelf at home. “I’ve stopped being surprised by the people who actually want their tissue or silicone, and if it’s something that’s doable, I’m happy to comply,” he says. Why do patients make these requests? “The reasons are really endless.” Can you take body parts home after surgery? Instead of resting or mentally preparing the day before her endometriosis surgery, Paul, the midwife who brought her fallopian tubes home, spent the day on the phone. She recalls being transferred between hospital employees, waiting for callbacks, and explaining, once again, her request to take her fallopian tubes home. She understood that the institution had protocols and concerns about liability. She was willing to sign paperwork, she said, but she couldn’t accept leaving without her tubes. “If they can’t be inside of me,” she recalls telling a hospital representative, “I’m taking them with me on the outside.” She explained their connection to her daughter, as well as the art she wanted to make. She asked what would happen if she didn’t take them home, and says she was told they would go to pathology and eventually be incinerated. That possibility made her more determined. “I do not consent,” she recalls saying, “to any of that happening to my organs.” Power says she intervened on Paul’s behalf, helping secure permission from hospital administrators and the pathology team. In her experience, getting tissue released has required advance conversations and paperwork, with requirements varying among the hospitals where she’s worked. A surgeon’s agreement alone hasn’t always been enough. At Ochsner Health in Louisiana, returning specimens is a familiar request, says Dr. Rebecca Phillips, chair of pathology and laboratory medicine services. Most patients don’t ask, but the system has a process for those who do. The first priority is completing the medical work: examining what was removed, making a diagnosis, and getting that information to the patient’s care team. “We want to make sure that we provide a diagnosis, we take care of whatever they need, and then we move forward to how can you keep it and how is that safe,” she says. Patients should make their wishes known in advance, Phillips says. At Ochsner, requested specimens are set aside in a lockbox rather than sent through the usual disposal process. Patients—or someone authorized to collect the material for them—must show identification and complete the required paperwork. Other hospitals may handle the process differently. “You won’t find the exact same standard operating procedure from hospital to hospital,” she says. Taking tissue home also raises a separate question: Should it be examined for signs of disease first? Paul says she declined pathological examination of her tubes, a decision Power confirms. Power says the possibility of missing a malignancy was one of the hospital’s concerns about releasing unexamined tissue. Paul’s arrangement was specific to her care; keeping a specimen and deciding which tests it needs are separate questions to discuss with your medical team. Having tissue examined doesn’t necessarily mean losing the chance to keep it. Pathologists are physicians who examine specimens to help diagnose disease and guide care. They may open an organ, cut it into sections, and take small samples to look at under a microscope, Phillips explains. If tissue remains after the necessary testing, it may be available to return. A small biopsy, however, might be used entirely for diagnosis. There’s also a distinction between leftover tissue in a specimen jar and the tissue blocks and microscope slides prepared for testing. Phillips says Ochsner holds leftover specimens for two weeks after the pathologist completes the diagnostic report, in case additional questions arise. Its accreditation requirements call for keeping slides and tissue blocks for 10 years. Those materials may be sent to another medical institution for further evaluation, she says; they aren’t simply handed over as keepsakes. On the morning of Paul’s surgery, two nurses approached her in pre-op with a question: Why did she want to keep her fallopian tubes? “I’m gonna make a really badass art project,” she told them. When Paul woke up after surgery, she had a question: “Where are my tubes?” Her fiancé showed her the containers. “They’re right here, baby,” she recalls him saying. A couple of days later, Paul sat with her daughter and her fiancé’s daughter and opened the containers. They looked at the tubes together. The young women, she says, were fascinated. How surgical souvenirs are preserved Preserving a body part can mean bringing a hazardous chemical home. Agullo says he’s returned removed tissue in containers of formalin, a preservative containing formaldehyde that can irritate the eyes, skin, and airways and is toxic if swallowed. Some patients later told him they kept the jars on a bookshelf or dresser. He tells them to keep the containers closed and out of children’s reach. Ochsner takes a different approach. Its laboratory uses formalin to preserve tissue for examination, but removes that chemical before returning a specimen. Staff follow a written procedure to treat the material, rinse it, and transfer it into saline, Phillips says. “We don’t let it go home,” she says of formalin. Paul’s tubes went home in saline, which Power emphasizes is not a preservation medium. Paul says she has since dehydrated them. Her artwork is still in progress: a clear, shadow-box-style frame incorporating the tubes, dried tropical flowers she gathers on her morning walks, and some of her menstrual blood. Her fiancé is collaborating with her. They haven’t chosen where to display it, but Paul wants it “someplace good, like really visible.” When she imagines looking at the finished piece, she thinks of her daughter—and what it took to bring the tubes home. “Fighting to keep them because they’re mine and nobody else’s and I get to keep them,” she says. She also feels “gratefulness for these badass women” who supported her along the way. Power hopes more clinicians will take these requests seriously. “If it’s an important thing to them,” she says, “it should be an important thing to us as providers as well.” For Emily, the jar on her bedroom table is “like a hunting trophy”—but instead of something dying, it’s a reminder of what she survived.

items.originalTitle: Xi, Trump, and Putin Summit Makes History but Not Much Else
items.author: Charlie Campbell
items.title: Xi, Trump, and Putin Summit Makes History but Not Much Else
items.summary: Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump pose for photos as they arrive for a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, 2026. —Vyacheslav Prokofyev—Pool/AFP/Getty Images It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.” Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC). The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.” It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.” It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.” Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.” Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine. That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.” Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke. In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959. Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway. Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling. “Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy. Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad. Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.” Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said. Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy. “The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.” But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity. Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said. Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II. But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of that invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said. After 90 minutes, the trilateral ended without remarks, the three leaders departing in their respective limousines. But the winner was clear. “The summit showcases the U.S. President and Russian President are trying to curry favor with the Chinese President,” says Ali Wyne, a senior researcher for the International Crisis Group. “The optics are quite striking in that regard.”

items.summary: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
